## 1. Intro and what a rate limiter is
- A system design classic; a good place to start if new to SD
- Still popular at top companies
  - Asked a lot at Microsoft
  - Users recently report it at OpenAI too
- Definition
  - Controls how many requests a client can make in a time frame
  - Example: social media app, limit 100 requests per minute per user
- Purpose: protect the backend
  - Users can't spam thousands of requests
  - Spam could take the system down or make it unusable for others

## 2. Delivery framework
- Hello Interview delivery framework, step by step
  1. Requirements: functional (features) + non-functional (qualities)
  2. Core entities: the nouns; tables, resources exchanged in APIs
  3. API or system interface
     - Rate limiter is a backend component; client doesn't call it directly
     - So focus on the system interface
  4. Data flow: sometimes useful; skipped here
  5. High-level design: boxes and arrows that satisfy the functional requirements
     - Get a minimal working design down early
  6. Deep dives: layer on complexity to satisfy non-functional requirements
     - Scale, low latency, fault tolerance

## 3. Functional requirements
- Backend components are more abstract than user-facing apps, but still clear
- Listed in the order a request arrives
  1. Identify clients by user ID, IP, or API key
     - Must know who it is to know how many requests they already made
  2. Limit requests based on configurable rules (the most important one)
     - Example rule: 100 requests per minute, maybe per endpoint
  3. Return proper error headers and status codes
     - Not an ambiguous 500
     - Tell them they're rate limited, plus metadata on what to do next

## 4. Scale questions
- Before NFRs: always check in with the interviewer about scale
- Ask: what am I rate limiting?
  - User-facing app like Facebook?
  - Developer tooling?
  - Between internal microservices?
- Most common answer: a user-facing social app
  - 100M DAU
  - 1M requests per second
- Aside on "server-side or client-side?"
  - Candidates often ask this; Evan found it confusing
  - Obviously server-side; client-side can be spoofed
    - You can't trust clients to limit themselves
  - He found most write-ups online start with that question
  - Realistic client-side use cases exist, but almost never asked
- Decision: server-side limiter, 100M DAU, 1M RPS

## 5. Non-functional requirements
- FR = what the system does; NFR = how it must do it (the "-ilities")
- Don't list every -ility
  - Everything you write you are expected to address in the design
  - Pick the ones most relevant and interesting
- CAP first
  - Partition tolerance is a must
  - Choose: strong consistency (every read sees latest write) or availability (eventual)
  - Choice: availability over consistency
    - Example: a new rule is propagating
    - Better the limiter keeps working on outdated rules briefly
    - Than going offline until all rules propagate
    - It protects the system, so it must stay up
- Low latency rate limit checks, under 10 ms
  - A weaker candidate writes "low latency" only
  - Interviewer asks: what do you mean?
  - A good candidate quantifies and qualifies
    - "Low latency rate limit checks, under 10 ms"
  - Why it matters: the limiter adds time to every user request
- Scalable to 1M RPS
- Purpose of FR + NFR: a contract with the interviewer
  - If you do all six well, you should leave confident you passed
  - Check in: anything missing or to change?

## 6. Core entities
- Less important for backend components; don't skip, do it in under a minute
- Request: the incoming request
- Client: who is making it (IP, user ID, API key)
- Rules: e.g. 100 requests per user per second

## 7. System interface
- System interface, not API
  - Users call the social app's API (e.g. get posts)
  - We check the limiter, likely via RPC or an internal call
- One function

```text
isRequestAllowed(clientId, ruleId) -> {
  passes: boolean,
  remaining: number,   // requests left if it passes
  resetTime: timestamp // depends on algorithm
}
```

## 8. HLD: where the limiter lives
- Method: go through FRs one by one
- Two key questions first
  1. Where should the limiter live in the architecture?
     - Determines what info it can access and how it integrates
  2. How should we identify clients?
     - Ensures the right limits apply to each user
  - Linked: placement affects available client info; identity affects placement
- Base system: Client -> Gateway -> Microservices (social media app)
- Option 1: inside each microservice (in application code)
  - Server checks local memory counts, updates, allows or rejects
  - Pro: extremely fast; in memory, no network calls, no dependencies
  - Con: no global picture
    - Request 1 hits service 1, request 2 hits service 2
    - Each sees one request; globally there were two
  - Lack of coordination makes it a poor option
- Option 2: dedicated rate limiter service
  - Each microservice asks it first: "am I allowed to process this?"
  - Pro: solves global coordination
  - Con: an extra network hop on every request
    - Admittedly fairly minimal
    - But tight latency requirement; overhead probably not worth it
- Option 3: at the edge, in the API gateway or load balancer
  - What most production systems use
  - Every request hits the limiter before routing
  - Analogy: bouncer at the club
    - Troublemakers turned away at the door, not after getting inside
  - Limitations
    - Scale: handled later in deep dives
    - Context: only info in the HTTP request
      - Headers, URL, IP, basic auth tokens
      - No deeper business logic or database access
  - Example: premium users get 10x higher limits
    - Still doable if premium status is encoded in the request
    - Typically via the JWT in the headers
  - Microservices then focus only on serving requests

## 9. HLD: identifying clients
- What makes a client unique: user ID, IP address, or API key
- Ask the interviewer
  - Are all users authenticated?
  - Is this a developer API requiring an API key?
- Most impressive answer: a combination, in layers
  - Authenticated users get higher limits than anonymous IPs
  - Premium users even more
  - Shows understanding of real-world systems
- Example layered rules
  - Alice: 1,000 requests per second
  - Any IP: 100 requests per second
  - An API: 50,000 requests per second
- All identified from the request, usually headers

## 10. HLD: algorithms
- FR2 is the heart: the algorithm that allows or rejects
- In SD (unlike LLD), the algorithm is not usually the main focus
  - Know options, weigh trade-offs, justify the choice
  - Likely no need to implement, not even pseudocode
- Four worth knowing, simplest first

### 10.1 Fixed window counter
- N requests per window, e.g. 100 per minute
- Per-user counter that resets at the start of each window
- Over the limit in the window: reject
- Diagram: 3 allowed per window, 4th rejected
- Pro: trivial; a hash table of client -> (counter, window start)

```json
{
  "alice:12:00:00": 100,
  "alice:12:01:00": 5,
  "bob:12:00:00": 20,
  "charlie:12:00:00": 0,
  "dave:12:00:00": 54,
  "eve:12:00:00": 0,
  "frank:12:00:00": 12
}
```

- Con 1: boundary effect
  - 100 requests at 12:01:59, 100 more at 12:02:00
  - 200 requests in 2 seconds
- Con 2: starvation
  - Use 100 at 12:01:01, then wait 59 seconds for any request

### 10.2 Sliding window log
- Smooths out fixed window issues
- Track a rolling window over the last minute
  - E.g. only 100 requests in the last rolling minute
- Tracks the exact time of each request: perfect accuracy
  - Eliminates boundary effect and burst problem
- Typically implemented with a heap or a deque
- Con: a lot more memory per user
  - More instances, more expensive

### 10.3 Sliding window counter
- Fixes the log's memory with a mild optimization
- Keep two counters: previous fixed window, current window
- Estimate the true sliding window by weighting by position in current window
- Example
  - Previous minute (1:00–1:01): 8 requests
  - Current minute: 42 s in (70%), 6 requests so far
  - Estimate = 6 + 30% of 8 = 8.4
  - Limit 10: 8.4 < 10, so pass
- Pro: much better accuracy than fixed window; two integers per user
- Con: an approximation
  - Assumes requests are evenly spread across windows, which may not hold
- Decent if you can accept the approximation

### 10.4 Token bucket (chosen)
- Arguably the most popular; the one chosen here
- Each client has a bucket of tokens
  - Bucket size = burst capacity
  - Tokens added at a steady refill rate
  - Each request consumes one token; none left = reject
- Two things handled nicely
  - Bucket size handles bursts (start with 100 = burst of 100)
  - Refill rate is the steady requests per time unit
- Example
  - Bucket holds 100 tokens: bursts up to 100
  - Refill 10 tokens per minute: steady 10 requests per minute
  - Client can make 100 immediately, then waits at the slower rate
- Pro: sustained load via refill rate, bursts via capacity
- Shockingly simple: track tokens + last refill time per client
- Challenge: choosing bucket size and refill rate, handling cold starts

## 11. HLD: storing state in Redis + race condition
- Each bucket tracks: current token count, last refill timestamp
- State must be shared across all gateway instances
  - Production has many gateways
  - Otherwise same problem as per-microservice limiters
- Pull state into an in-memory cache like Redis
- Flow
  1. Request comes in
  2. Gateway fetches tokens and last refill from Redis
     - `HMGET alice:bucket tokens last_refill` (multiple fields, one command)
  3. Update count based on rate and last refill
     - Last refill 30 s ago, rate 1 token/s: add 30
     - Count was 20, now 50
  4. Respond pass or fail based on tokens after refill > 0
  5. Update bucket status
     - Write back new token count and last refill = now
- Race condition
  - Gateway A and B each get one of Alice's requests
  - Both read Redis: value is 1
  - No refill since last check; both see 1 > 0; both accept
  - Both write; one overwrites the other
  - Read A, read B, write A, write B
  - The read and write for each must be atomic
- Fix
  - In Postgres or similar: transactions with locking
  - Redis: supports atomic transactions and is single-threaded
  - Use Lua scripting
    - HMGET + HSET to update tokens, all in one Lua script
    - Goes over the wire, reads and writes in one instance, returns pass/fail
    - Atomic: one does everything, the other waits until it finishes

## 12. HLD: responses, 429 and headers
- Decision: on limit exceeded, reject immediately or queue?
- Choice: fail fast, send failure immediately, no queue
  - Queueing a feed request: user waits, thinks it's broken, retries
  - Backlog grows; bigger issue
  - Niche cases where queueing fits: batch systems that can wait
    - Usually intra-service communication
  - For an interactive fast API, fail fast is common and right
- HTTP status: 429 Too Many Requests
  - Standard code for exactly this; interviewers expect you to know it
- Best-practice headers

```text
X-RateLimit-Limit: ceiling for that request (e.g. "100")
X-RateLimit-Remaining: requests left in current window (e.g. "0")
X-RateLimit-Reset: when the limit resets, Unix timestamp (e.g. "1640995200")
Retry-After: 60
```

  - "Remaining" depends on the algorithm's notion of a window; can get funky
- Don't memorize the header names
  - Say: "429 with headers telling them when to retry and how many remain"

## 13. Deep dive: scaling to 1M RPS
- Deep dives: go through NFRs one by one (out of order here)
- Single Redis instance won't scale
  - On the order of 100K ops/s, depending on hardware
  - Each check is two ops (HMGET + HSET)
  - So maybe 50K requests per second
- Need to shard
  - Spread keys across Redis instances
  - Alice on instance 1, Bob on instance 2
  - 1M / 50K = 20 instances at least; tell interviewer a bit more for overhead
- How to shard
  - Gateway must know which instance holds Alice's bucket
  - Random instance: may not have Alice
  - Replicate all data everywhere: same problem, memory is limited
    - In memory, e.g. 64 GB, maybe go up to 100-something GB
- Shard by client ID (user ID, IP, or API key)
  - Consistent hashing is one option
  - In reality, with Redis, use Redis Cluster
    - Manages sharding for you
    - Not consistent hashing; uses hash slots
    - "Something like 60,000 hash slots" distributed across nodes
    - Handles mapping user to slot to node
- Main point for the interview: multiple instances, so shard

## 14. Deep dive: availability and fault tolerance
- What if a Redis node holding Alice's bucket fails?
  - Alice can't be rate limited
- First: what to do if it fails
  - Fail open: limiter down, every request gets through
  - Fail closed: limiter down, no requests get through
  - Common terminology for rate limiters; discuss with interviewer
- Social network case
  - Fail open: no longer protecting services
    - Limits exist for DB, cache, CPU/GPU capacity
    - Services may die one by one: cascading failure, even worse
  - Fail closed: site is down, users report "Facebook is down"
  - No right or wrong answer
  - Typically fail closed
    - The limiter's job is to protect the backend
    - If down, take the strictest protection: reject everything
- More sophisticated in real production
  - Keep some state in the gateway's own memory
  - Fall back to a local fixed window counter while Redis is down
  - No cross-gateway coordination, but it's temporary
  - Better than failing open or closed
- Second: prevent failure and recover fast
  - Replicas: replication factor of one or two per shard
  - Writes propagate to replica; on failure, replica is promoted
  - Redis Cluster supports this
  - Uses async replication: not perfect
    - Trade-off: availability over consistency
    - A write lost before replication: Alice at 99 instead of 100
    - She gets one extra request; no big deal
- Key to HA + fault tolerance: sharding and replicas; Redis Cluster does both

## 15. Deep dive: low latency
- Every check needs a network round trip to Redis
  - Redis ops are typically sub-millisecond
  - Network overhead can be several ms per request
- Most important optimization: connection pooling
  - Gateway keeps a pool of persistent TCP connections to Redis
  - Eliminates the TCP handshake overhead
    - "Can sometimes be 20 to even 50 ms depending on network distance"
  - Most Redis clients do this automatically
    - "I don't know a single one that doesn't"
  - May need to tune pool size by request volume and Redis response time
  - Tell the interviewer you know the client likely handles it
- Geographic distribution
  - Gateway and limiter close to users
  - Tokyo users: gateway in Asia/Japan
  - Redis co-located with the gateway, ideally same data center, next to each other

## 16. Deep dive: dynamic rule configuration
- Common in interviews
- So far rules assumed static
  - Baked in at gateway deploy (refill rate, bucket size)
  - Changing them means redeploying the gateway
- Production: rules configurable, different per user type (premium, etc.)
- Option 1: gateway polls the database
  - E.g. every 20 seconds
  - Delay (20 s, 10 s, 5 s); 1 s burns gateway CPU on constant polling
- Option 2: store rules in Redis
  - Don't need the DB; each shard holds the rules key
  - Poll periodically, or check rules on every rate limit check
  - Adds operations to every check, raises latency; rules rarely change
- Option 3 (best): push-based configuration
  - ZooKeeper ("a bit outdated nowadays, I must admit") or etcd (more in vogue)
  - Built for distributed configuration management
  - Gateway fetches rules on startup, keeps them in memory
  - Subscribes to watch for changes over a persistent TCP connection
  - Changes are pushed; gateway updates in memory
  - No extra latency or network calls per request, no polling

## 17. Level expectations
- Mid-level: ~80% breadth, 20% depth
  - Understand the algorithms; choose and justify
  - May not code them perfectly, but conceptually understand them
  - Know the limiter belongs at the edge
  - Propose shared global state (Redis, Memcached) and justify it
  - Answer probes: single Redis limits, what if it goes down
  - Reach reasonable answers with interviewer leading
- Senior: much more proactive
  - Say proactively a single Redis node won't cut it, with the math
  - How many shards, and what to shard on
  - Proactively discuss fault tolerance, overload, fail open/closed
- Staff: asked less often; "kind of on the easier or medium side maybe"
  - Proactively lead through nearly everything above
  - Steer to areas you know deeply
    - E.g. Redis Cluster experience; mis-sizing the connection pool and why size matters
    - Proactively spot the race condition and explain Lua scripting

- Text version, assembled from the talk
  - Framework: Requirements, Core Entities, API/Interface, (Data Flow), HLD, Deep Dives
  - FR: identify users by id/IP/API key; limit by configurable rules; proper headers and codes
  - Scale: 100M DAU, 1M RPS
  - NFR: availability >> consistency; checks < 10 ms; scalable to 1M RPS
  - Entities: Request, Client (IP, userId, API key), Rules (100 r/s)
  - Interface: `isRequestAllowed(clientId, rulesId) -> { passes, remaining, resetTime }`

```text
            ZooKeeper (etcd): rules
                 | watch for changes
Client <--429-- Gateway [rules in memory] --> Microservice 1/2/3
                 |
          Redis x 20 (50K rps each; 1M / 50K = 20)
                 | async replication
          Redis replicas         (fail open / fail closed)
```
